title: 9 years of game dev 100x accelerated thanks to AI
author: bgilb
selftext:
My instagram is full of people bashing or debating about AI. I think its insane, considering AAA studios using AI don't get harassed about their usage of AI. The stigma promotes lying. Everyone wants an "artisanal only" game that took 25 years to develop. At this point I don't care if my steam disclaimer flatly just says this game is not possible without AI, so judge it however you want.   
  
I think what it's really about is the fact that a solo dev can now almost compete with an entire studio, and that scares people. I've been working on this game for 9 years, have a good amount of indie game dev experience, so I don't think the game is vibe coded at all, and the uses of gen AI are fairly limited. The quality speaks for itself.

The game is called Unfallen and is a crazy combination of survival+zombie+kenshi+ultima online and is basically my dream game. The video shows maybe 40% of the playable features in the game.

comments.author: Ok_Feedback4200
comments.body:
There's no future in gaming without AI. It's as clear as day. Players will wake up to this realization too one day. Or they will be forced to go back to sloppy human made games with zero innovation and a bag full of bugs.

Big IT and Tech companies don't write their code either anymore. Their programmers are busy with other tasks.. As a 3D artist myself, I like that I can automate big parts of my animation work now while retaining control. It's like I can design and animate using my brain, like I always wanted... (though actual design is still very shit when it's made by AI... so atleast design is still very much alive today and it doesn't feel like AI has touched it much). It's still the same software, doing the same stuff, just UI is no longer needed as scripts are the main way to work.... I don't think AI killed design or art. I even think it helped revive it a bit. New design styles are emerging, and people are appreciating real human craft more than ever.

Regarding development, I have a bit of experienec in python and C#, but very little. Now, with AI, I'm able to start developing my games again, something I've done about 10 years ago and never picked up again when I faced my first issues inside Unity... Mad respect to every OG programmer that came before AI. I don't know how you people did it. Maybe it's a collective effort to create all of this we have in the digital space now. But I also think we can reach such complex and awesome systems now, that you'd need to be a bit autistic to actually create all that code yourself. It's just not possible for most human beings.

So we either limit how big and good games can get, and enjoy the pure pre-ai era games... Or we embrace it and await for all the new awesome titles that are awaiting us. 100% in 2-3 years we will start seeing games we wouldn't have thought would be possible. Imagine what a team of 10 experiences and passionate developers/artists could do, each with a claude max sub and a shared goal in mind... They won't create the GTA 7, but I wouldn't be surprised if something at the level of GTA 4 or GTA 5 would start appearing soon from small teams.

replies.author: Ok_Feedback4200

Good that you enjoy the labour. Personally, I've been animating for more than a decade. I still love animation and the craft behind it. Love everything about 3D too. Spent more than a decade learning ins and outs of how everythings built in 3D. Now with AI I can be much more productive with my time. As long as I remain in full creative control, I don't have a problem using AI to optimize my workflows. Working in 3D has always been about the latest tech and newest tools. We used to rig things only manually. Animate manually too.. then came mixamo rigs and free motion capture apps. Now tools are evolving further and making things in 3D becomes easier. Why is that a bad thing, I don't know. The output quality will still depend on the user and his input. Code is the same in my view.

I'm not sure how it is when you are a programmer. I understand coding can be fun, I have tried creating Unity games on my own before and I had a lot of fun doing it. C# was super fun and quite easy to get into.. But again, let's be real.. You're a software developer. Would you say you write better code than opus? Or that you can solve the problems in the code that opus wouldn't? I been listening to some gamedev podcasts and honestly I think being a traditional programmer is much more depressing now compared to the creative jobs. But then again, o many opportunities now arise to create stuff that you wouldn't have been able to before simply because of time constraints..

replies.author: oof-plap
replies.body:
This looks like code-as-graphics, I know because it looks very similar to what I'm working on too haha.

The dither animation when walls fade out is *identical*. Good things to look for are lowpoly shapes with "noise" textures on them, its convenient that a lot of people pick that style - because AI is *quite good at it, and you don't have to leave Claude to generate it*. 

The shadows also show the wonky "sun" placement which leads to quite compromised/"wrong" looking shadows.

This isn't a diss it's just the things you notice.

FYI,  Voxel just means **Vo**lume Pi**xel**, in other words, a 3D pixel.  

Minecraft narrowly defines that volume as a cube.  It doesn't have to be just a cube.

replies.author: Kolaps_
replies.body:
What I'm saying is that the developer of Dwarf Fortress is still working on his game because that's how he chose to work: over the long term. The first four years of development weren't even full-time, and the game has been profitable for a long time.

So using Dwarf Fortress as an example to justify your argument about spending 25 years developing a game is dishonest. It's a game that's being developed over such a long period by its creator's own choice, not out of necessity.

And that's exactly my issue with discussions about AI, especially in the video game industry. Most people seem incapable of simply discussing the reality of what this medium is, and what the various AI tools actually involve.

They exaggerate things on one side and downplay them on the other.

Of course people don't know how to properly scope a game. That's a skill, an actual area of expertise, and a job a part of the job of a game director and producer (and any supervisor). But bringing up scope doesn't justify your position of saying, "I don't want to spend 25 years working on a game."

If you get no enjoyment out of developing games, if the process of development itself doesn't interest you, then just stay a player.

This is a fundamental aspect of game development: if you'd rather play than create, then don't create. And if you genuinely enjoy creating, then the prospect of working on something for a long time shouldn't put you off.

comments.author: relic1882
comments.body:
I think a lot of the problem with people is they just use a blanket statement like "It's taking jobs away fuck AI!" I see nothing wrong with using available tools to create your vision, as long as it's YOUR vision. Even if someone uses AI to do all the programming work that they can't do, it frees up more time for you to be a director and steer the project into what you want it to be. It's like when a movie director gets all the credit for making a hit movie. He didn't write it, act in it or create the sets himself. He made sure all the pieces came together for the vision he had. 

Just for reference here, I do all my own coding and try my hardest to create characters on my own in my original project. But I use AI to help me prototype systems quickly or have it analyze if there's a bug I can't figure out at all. I don't rely on it, but it's very handy.

Another example is a level I made has hundreds of tombstones in one area in the background. I told AI to take every one of them, tilt, scale and lean them with random values within a certain percentage. Now all my tombstones have a varied look, making the level subtly look that much better and it only took it 30 seconds compared to me doing it one at a time for hours. I act like a director.

Well I try to plan as much and as detailed as possible in advance and have a clear direction, reference pictures and I use Gemini to create paint overs of my scenes to improve iteration. 
I came down from 7-15 iterations to about 5 depending on the asset or scene. 
I envision myself playing the game and try to think of every nuance of it then I discuss with ai and iterate. 
I have a single agent chat, the curator, opus on very high who doesn't code but makes sure that all other agents stay on track. If he reviews something that is not up to par, he will inform the agent and iteration happens mostly automatically. But still it's not enough, all the agents need my input and my corrections. It needs a lot of fine-tuning to get a nice result that looks handmade (in my eyes)

I try to hide my shortcomings through perspective and artstyle 😆

replies.author: alphapussycat
replies.body: I suspect you're offloading decision making to the AI though. Not done anything, but I'm pretty sure the bottleneck is the human decisions and planning.

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body: No I take a walk with the dog and play everything in my head. The bottleneck is the price of tokens.   At least for me. Ai does make decisions but only in regards to code and even there I have very strict rules. Over the years I fucked up more then enough projects

comments.author: Various-Patience1842
comments.body:
This looks absolutely amazing! And who can say this isn't creativity?

Why is someone who has the financial resources to buy 1,000 assets and hire 50 people to develop a game praised for their work, while a solo developer using AI is somehow doing something wrong?

AI allows people to create games of much higher quality, and those games still reflect the creator's vision, as long as they've put enough time and effort into development.

And you've clearly put a lot of both into this project.

Wishing you the best of luck with your game!

comments.body:
Hey do you mind sharing some insight into making life-sized pixel characters (and animating them!), or are they 3d with some sort of post-processing?

I can't get anything usable out of Claude, most free assets or pixel generators make these "Chibby" size characters that I dont want

replies.author: bgilb
replies.body:
Like 95% of my art assets are not really gen AI. The characters are 3D with a pixel art shader. My engine only has a few things that are true 3D, the rest is my custom engine which is hard to explain.

My advice is that gen AI is still severely limited, so don't really depend on it. Its horrible at animations, and almost all 3D characters.
